query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: For multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution ("high-entropy") nanoparticles with an FCC lattice, long-term structural and chemical stability between 773–1173 K is primarily governed by the magnitude of configurational lattice distortion, quantified by the atomic-radius variance parameter δ. Particles whose global composition provides δ ≥ 4 % will suppress bulk/surface segregation and coarsening, whereas particles with δ ≤ 2 % will partially decompose into secondary phases and sinter under identical thermal or catalytic conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: ≈10 nm FCC CoNiFeCr high-entropy alloy nanoparticles produced by a colloidal reduction route, fully single-phase and chemically homogeneous before testing.
generation.intervention: Raise δ from ≈1.5 % to ≈5 % by isovalently substituting 5–10 at % of a large-radius refractory element (e.g., Nb or Zr) at the expense of Co and Ni, without changing the average valence electron concentration.
generation.conditions: Static 10 vol % H₂ / Ar atmosphere, 1 bar, 900 °C (1173 K) for 50 h (representative of high-temperature catalysis); identical temperature ramp rate (10 K min⁻¹) and cooling profile for all samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Root-mean-square local lattice distortion amplitude that raises the activation barrier for atomic diffusion within the solid solution.
generation.mechanism: A larger atomic-size mismatch generates higher local elastic strain energy and broadens the distribution of nearest-neighbour bond lengths. This increases vacancy-formation and migration enthalpies, slowing long-range diffusion that would otherwise drive elemental segregation, phase separation, and particle coarsening. Entropic stabilization remains comparable, so the net effect is enhanced thermal and chemical robustness when δ is above a critical threshold (~4 %).
generation.predicted_outcome: After 50 h at 900 °C: (i) High-δ nanoparticles retain a single-phase FCC pattern by XRD with peak broadening <10 % relative to the as-made state; STEM-EDX line scans show <10 % deviation from the initial bulk composition across the particle; average particle diameter increases by <25 %. (ii) Low-δ (baseline) nanoparticles show additional BCC or σ-phase reflections, >30 % surface enrichment of the lowest-melting element, and >100 % growth in mean particle size.
generation.boundary: Applies to 5–20 nm FCC high-entropy nanoparticles in inert or mildly reducing atmospheres up to ≈1100 °C and containing ≤10 at % oxophilic elements; may not hold for strongly oxidising environments, for particle sizes <3 nm (melting point depression), or when large negative enthalpies of mixing dominate over lattice-distortion effects.
generation.uncertainty: Other factors (e.g., cohesive energy differences, electronic effects, short-range ordering) also influence diffusion; the exact δ threshold may vary with composition. Absence of direct diffusion-barrier measurements leaves mechanistic details partly inferential.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two nanoparticle batches: (A) Co20Ni20Fe20Cr20Mn20 (low-δ) and (B) Co17Ni17Fe20Cr20Nb6Mn20 (high-δ). Confirm identical initial size and single-phase FCC structure via XRD and STEM-EDX. Subject both to the stated 900 °C H₂/Ar anneal for 50 h. Quench, then characterise by (1) synchrotron XRD for phase identification and peak broadening, (2) aberration-corrected STEM-EDX mapping for elemental distributions, and (3) TEM size statistics.
measurements: Elemental maps and radial composition profiles (STEM-EDX)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, after heat treatment, the high-δ sample (B) shows equal‐or-greater phase separation, elemental segregation (>30 %) or particle coarsening (>100 %) compared with the low-δ sample (A), or if sample (A) remains fully single-phase and size-stable while (B) degrades, the hypothesis is falsified.
